items.readable_text:
Content:
To solve a two-term quadratic equation like [MATH: x^2 - 7x = 0] where there is no constant term, we can factor out the variable and apply the zero-product rule.

Content:
Factoring out the variable, we have:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x^2 - 7x &= 0 \
x(x - 7) &= 0
}]

Content:
We apply the zero product rule to get

Content:
[MATH: x=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x-7=0,]

Content:
which in turn gives

Content:
[MATH: x=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=7.]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=0,7.]

Content:
To check that these solutions are correct, we can substitute them back into the original equation:

Content:
[MATH: x|= 0|x|= 7; ⇓|⇓; x^{2} − 7x|= 0|x^{2} − 7x|= 0; 0^{2} − 7(0)|= 0|7^{2} − 7(7)|= 0; 0 − 0|= 0|49 − 49|= 0; 0|= 0✓|0|= 0✓]

Content:
Warning: It's tempting to solve the equation by dividing by [MATH: x,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − 7x|= 0; (x^{2} − 7x)/(x)|= (0)/(x); x − 7|= 0; x|= 7]

Content:
However, if we do that, we lose the solution [MATH: x=0.] So, when solving equations, never divide by a variable because the variable could be zero, and division by zero is not allowed. Instead, try to factor the variable in the equation.

sections.normalized_html:
First, we move all of the terms to the left-hand side and then factor: [MATH: \eqalign{ 3p^2 &= 5p \[3pt] 3p^2 - 5p &= 0 \[3pt] p(3p - 5) &= 0 }]

So, by the zero product rule, we have

[MATH: p=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad 3p-5=0,]

which in turn gives

[MATH: p=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad p=\dfrac{5}{3}.]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: p=0,\dfrac{5}{3}.]

[MATH: 6x^{2} + 2x − 2|= 8x^{2} − x − 2; 6x^{2} + 2x − 2 − (8x^{2} − x − 2)|= 0; 6x^{2} + 2x − 2 − 8x^{2} + x + 2|= 0; (6x^{2} − 8x^{2}) + (2x + x) + (− 2 + 2)|= 0; − 2x^{2} + 3x + 0|= 0; − 2x^{2} + 3x|= 0; x(− 2x + 3)|= 0]

So, by the zero product rule, we have

[MATH: x=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad -2x + 3=0,]

which in turn gives

[MATH: x=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=\dfrac{3}{2}.]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=0,\dfrac{3}{2}.]
